analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue pesticide makers under state law for failing to warn about health risks.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2026 with sponsors from both parties, the bill was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal pesticide law, a company's pesticide being registered and its label approved by the EPA can shield it from state lawsuits claiming it failed to warn people about health dangers. This bill would change that: it says federal registration and label approval are not a defense to a state law claim, only evidence to be weighed. It would let people bring failure-to-warn suits under state law, would let companies update warning labels quickly when new health information emerges, and would apply to lawsuits already in progress. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to pesticides who believe the products harmed their health and that the maker hid or downplayed the risks. The bill applies to lawsuits already pending, so current plaintiffs — including those alleging weed-killer products like glyphosate-based herbicides caused cancer — could continue in state court even if a court had thrown their case out under the federal preemption defense. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pesticide exposure victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds language to federal pesticide law saying that a pesticide's federal registration and EPA-approved labeling 'shall not be construed as a defense to any State law claim.' [S2]
It preserves state law claims that are consistent with federal misbranding standards, so a person who says a label failed to warn of health effects can take that claim to a state court or jury. [S2]
It applies to any civil action pending on or after the date of enactment, regardless of when the exposure happened, reopening suits that were dismissed on preemption grounds. [S2]

It also creates a duty for pesticide makers to address newly obtained misbranding information — including whistleblower disclosures, independent studies, and incident data — by amending their labels without waiting for prior EPA approval. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers, who would face state court juries and damages in failure-to-warn cases they can currently defend against by pointing to federal registration. Industry backers warn of higher costs or fewer products available to farmers; the bill text itself does not restrict any pesticide from being sold. [S2]

drawbacks.text: Pesticide makers and farm groups argue that products approved by EPA under a single national standard should not be second-guessed by state-by-state juries applying different warning rules, and that litigation risk can lead companies to pull useful products from the market. This is the industry's standard objection to de-preempting federal pesticide law; it is a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge. [S2]

The bill applies retroactively to pending lawsuits 'regardless of the date on which the conduct' occurred, changing the legal rules for companies mid-dispute and potentially reviving cases that courts had already dismissed. [S2]

The bill allows registrants to change labels without prior EPA approval when new health information emerges, which EPA could later disapprove — a speed-versus-certainty tradeoff in how warnings reach consumers. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: people who say a pesticide maker hid health risks get their day in court, which they largely cannot have now because federal registration and an approved label block state failure-to-warn suits. The main cost falls on pesticide manufacturers, which is partly the point of a liability regime, though the industry's warning that litigation pressure could shrink the menu of farm chemicals is a real one, and the retroactivity provision is aggressive. On balance the bill shifts the risk of undisclosed harm from the people exposed to the companies that sell the product.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and the committee has not taken it up, so with the session ending in early January it is on track to die without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Paulina Luna introduced the bill on July 21, 2026, joined as original cosponsors by Reps. Rosa DeLauro, Thomas Massie, and Chellie Pingree. [S2]
It was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day and no further action has been taken. [S4]
The bill would reverse, in part, the effect of federal pesticide law under which EPA registration and label approval have shielded manufacturers from state failure-to-warn claims. [S2]
Its retroactivity clause would apply to lawsuits pending on or after enactment, regardless of when the conduct occurred. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers are better off: because the bill has not moved, federal registration and EPA-approved labels remain a defense against state failure-to-warn lawsuits, and no pending cases are reopened. The Agriculture Committee, which has not acted on it, and the industry it is friendliest to, benefit from that inaction.

for.name: Anna Paulina Luna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to preserve state failure-to-warn lawsuits against pesticide makers.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Glenn 'GT' Thompson (R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 21, 2026 and has not scheduled a markup or taken any further action on it.

against.name: Pesticide manufacturers (Bayer/Monsanto and peers)
against.what_they_did: Have publicly lobbied Congress for the opposite policy — a federal preemption shield that would bar state failure-to-warn suits over products like glyphosate-based weed killers.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, but the bill's five supporters split two Republicans and three Democrats, with no opposition yet on the record.

industries.industry: Pesticide manufacturers (Bayer/Monsanto, Corteva, Syngenta and peers)
industries.note: The bill strips away the manufacturers' strongest courtroom defense — that EPA registration and an approved label bar state failure-to-warn claims — and applies that change to cases already in progress. Their interest in keeping the shield runs directly against people seeking to sue over alleged undisclosed health harms. [S2]

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' law firms handling pesticide exposure cases
industries.note: Preserving state claims and making them apply to pending suits enlarges the pool of viable cases for lawyers who represent people alleging pesticide-related illness. Their gain tracks the public's gain in access to court. [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With the 119th Congress ending January 3, 2027, a five-month-old bill with four cosponsors sitting untouched in the House Agriculture Committee — the committee most aligned with the industry it targets — is very unlikely to get a markup or a floor vote before the session ends. Expect it to expire and need reintroduction in the next Congress.
